To give a short wedding toast in the right register.

Friday, 2 May 2030, evening. Elena and Dan have arrived from Iași. Dan wants to read out his speech for his son’s wedding. He prepared it with a French textbook from the eighties. Ioana listens, and Radu tries not to laugh.
Right. I’ll begin. “Ladies and gentlemen, allow me to express the immense joy that fills my father’s heart on this memorable day.”
Dad, it’s very beautiful. But it’s a bit… formal. It sounds like a president’s speech.
Formal? But my book says that is how one speaks to distinguished French people.
Dad, the guests are mates, colleagues, Lucia’s family… Nobody talks like that. Just say: “I’m super happy to be here.”
No, “super happy” is too familiar for a speech. Let’s say instead: “I’m very happy to be with you today.” That’s the standard register. Not too much, not too little.
“I’m very happy to be with you today.” All right. Next: “My son, whom I watched grow up, has found a wife of rare beauty and great virtue.”
(laughs) Virtue! Lucia will love that. Dad, you say: “My son has found a wonderful woman.” Full stop.
And my joke? I prepared a joke about the son-in-law and the mother-in-law.
Dad… Radu’s mother-in-law will be sitting in the front row. Save the joke for Iași.
All right. And the ending? “I kindly request that you raise your glasses in honour of the young couple.”
That’s perfect. For a toast, a little solemnity is good. Everyone will raise their glass.
And afterwards, Dad, you can say: “Come on, let’s eat!” Then everyone will understand you.
“On bouffe”? That’s not in my book. It isn’t rude, at least?
No, it’s familiar, not rude. But don’t say it in front of the mayor.
In speech, “tu es” becomes “t’es”, “il y a” becomes “y a”, “je ne sais pas” becomes “chais pas”.
French changes a lot according to the situation. The same thing is said differently with friends, with a stranger and in an official speech:
The STANDARD register is the safe one: it works almost everywhere. You need to UNDERSTAND the familiar one (films, friends, children), but use it with care.
Dropping “ne” is normal in spoken French, even among educated people. In writing (letters, official emails, exams) always keep it!
A FAMILIAR word (bouffer, boulot, mec) isn’t offensive; it’s just relaxed. A RUDE word (grossier) can shock. In dictionaries: “fam.” = familiar, “vulg.” = vulgar.
Learners often pick up slang from films and use it in the wrong context. “Mon boulot” in a job interview sounds unprofessional; say “mon travail” or “mon poste”.
You find it in literature, speeches, formal letters. A few signs:
I kindly request that you… (official letters)
That is how one speaks. (“l’on” instead of “on”, after “que, si, où”)
May I help you? (“puis-je” instead of “est-ce que je peux”)
Dan’s textbook isn’t wrong: these forms are correct. It’s just that at a young people’s wedding they sound like a tailcoat on the beach.
Je suis très ému(e) / heureux(se) d’être parmi vous.
Je me souviens du jour où…
Je vous souhaite tout le bonheur du monde.
Je vous propose de lever vos verres aux mariés !
I invite you to raise your glasses to the bride and groom!
In a job interview you say…
I’m very happy to be with you today.
Don’t worry, we’re going to eat well.

Le dernier 3 mai avant le mariage

On Thursday 1 May, at eight in the morning, Odile’s kitchen already smelled of cozonac. The grandmother had got up at five. She had found the flour, butter and eggs without asking where they were, as if she had always lived in that flat. Odile, in her dressing gown, watched from the doorway, a cup of coffee in her hand, fascinated.

The two women had no language in common, and yet they talked to each other non-stop. The grandmother spoke Romanian, Odile spoke French, and each answered what she thought she had understood. The most astonishing thing was that it worked. When the grandmother pointed at the oven raising her eyebrows, Odile immediately understood that it was too hot. And she was right.

Around ten, Radu came up with two little bunches of lily of the valley. It was the 1 May tradition; he had learned it three years earlier, when he gave lily of the valley to Hélène and Odile on the bench at Fourvière. He gave one to Odile and one to his grandmother. The grandmother smelled the flowers for a long time. “Mărgăritar,” she said. Odile repeated the word, with an impossible accent.

In the afternoon, at Saint-Exupéry airport, Radu, Lucia and Julien waited at the arrivals gate. The flight from Seville was twenty minutes late. Lucia couldn’t keep still. She wondered whether her grandmother had survived the journey, whether she had been afraid, whether she had prayed the whole flight. Radu held her hand so that she would stop pacing up and down.

Doña Carmen came out first, very pale, a rosary in her right hand, her bag clutched in her left. Behind her came don Manuel, in a light suit and a straw hat, his guitar on his back, smiling like a man who has just won a bet. Then Lucia’s parents, Antonio and Pilar, loaded with suitcases and boxes of wine.

Lucia ran to her grandmother. Doña Carmen hugged her, then declared, in Spanish, that it was the first and last time in her life she would get on a plane, and that she would walk back to Seville if she had to. Don Manuel laughed. According to him, she had slept half the flight, her head on his shoulder.

Don Manuel, on the other hand, had had an extraordinary flight. The flight attendant had agreed to let his guitar travel in the cabin, provided he kept it on his knees. Halfway through the flight, the pilot, who had heard that an old flamenco guitarist was on board, came to ask him for a song. Don Manuel played, at ten thousand metres, in front of a hundred and forty passengers.

“It was my highest concert,” he said in French, with his Parisian-cabaret accent. “And the audience was captive. Nobody could leave.” Doña Carmen rolled her eyes. She explained to Lucia that she hadn’t slept at all: she had only closed her eyes so as not to see her husband clowning around in front of strangers.

In the evening, Odile insisted that everyone come to dinner at her place. That evening the little flat on rue d’Austerlitz welcomed four countries, three languages and enough food to feed an army. The grandmother had made sarmale and cozonac. Pilar had brought ham, olives and gazpacho. Odile had made an apple tart, the only recipe she knew by heart.

The meeting between the grandmother and doña Carmen was the moment everyone had been waiting for. The two women looked each other up and down for a long time, like two generals before a battle. Then doña Carmen took out her rosary. The grandmother took a small wooden icon out of her bag. They showed each other their treasures, and nodded at the same time.

Then they sat side by side on the sofa and didn’t leave each other all evening. Lucia translated from Spanish into French, Radu from French into Romanian, and often the two grandmothers grew impatient and started talking to each other directly again, each in her own language. They laughed at the same moments. Nobody knew why.

At one point doña Carmen asked, through Lucia, where the grandmother’s husband was. There was a silence. The grandmother took out of her wallet an old black-and-white photo: a young man with a moustache, dancing in the middle of a circle of people. “Ion,” she said. “The best dancer in the village. He left us ten years ago.”

Don Manuel took the photo and looked at it for a long time. Then he picked up his guitar, without a word, and began to play. It wasn’t flamenco. It was a slow tune in three-four time that he was improvising. After a few bars, he held out his hand to the grandmother. She hesitated, then stood up. They danced in the middle of Odile’s living room, between the sofa and the table.

Doña Carmen watched her husband dance with another woman, and smiled. Then she said a sentence to Lucia, which Lucia translated, her voice trembling: “My grandmother says that a man who knows how to make a widow dance is a man who has understood life.” Odile, in her corner, took out a handkerchief. She didn’t hide it.

On Friday 2 May, Elena and Dan arrived from Iași, on the midday flight. Elena had brought her list of forty-three things, forty-two of which had been ticked. The forty-third was “Don’t cry at the town hall”. She already knew she would never tick it. Dan had his speech in the inside pocket of his jacket, printed in large type.

The meeting between Dan and Antonio, Lucia’s father, was a model of international communication. Dan held out his hand, declaring in the French of his old textbook: “Delighted to make your acquaintance, dear sir.” Antonio replied in Spanish with something nobody translated. They shook hands for a long time, with plenty of goodwill and zero understanding.

Then Antonio uttered a magic word: “Fútbol?” Dan’s face lit up. For the next two hours, the two fathers compared the Iași and Seville teams, the great matches of the nineties, names of players nobody else knew. They needed nothing but proper names and gestures. Elena and Pilar left them to it, relieved.

In the evening, while Dan was rehearsing his speech in front of Ioana and Radu in the kitchen, Julien and Karim were organising the stag night. Nothing extravagant: a dinner in a Lyon bouchon in the Vieux-Lyon, with Julien, Karim, Théo, Pierre Moreau, who had come from Annecy for the occasion, and Costel, who had been invited by the grandmother and didn’t want to miss anything.

In the bouchon, Radu spoke a French Ioana wouldn’t have recognised. “Honestly, guys, I’m scared stiff,” he admitted after the second glass. “Work’s fine. The hall’s fine. But this is something else.” Karim slapped him on the shoulder. “Don’t sweat it. Everyone’s scared stiff the night before. I threw up in the Rhône.” Théo, who was drinking apple juice, made mental notes.

Costel, who spoke almost no French, ended up standing to give a toast in Romanian, very long and very solemn. Radu translated as he went along. Costel spoke of the road, of borders, of all the grandmothers he had driven in twenty years, and of the bravest of them all, who was now sitting next to Odile, two streets away.

At eleven, Radu fell asleep on the table, his head between a plate of quenelles and a pot of cervelle de canut. His friends looked at him tenderly. Pierre Moreau paid the bill, Karim and Julien carried him to a taxi, and Costel insisted on sitting next to the driver, to keep an eye on the road.

Lucia, for her part, spent the evening in a flamenco bar in the Croix-Rousse with Chloé, Manon, Leïla and two cousins who had come from Salamanca. According to witnesses, she danced on a table, sang a sevillana with the bar owner, and called Radu three times to tell him she loved him. He didn’t answer. He was asleep on a plate of quenelles.

Chloé took advantage of the evening to teach the cousins from Salamanca a few essential words of familiar French. By midnight they could say “C’est trop bien”, “J’ai la flemme” and “Il est canon, ton mec”. Lucia made them promise never to use these expressions in front of the mayor, or Radu’s grandmother, or above all Dan, who might put them in his speech.

Saturday 3 May was a special day, and everyone knew it. Hélène would have been eighty-eight. It was also Julien and Ioana’s wedding anniversary, and the first anniversary of Hélène’s death. Odile had suggested that the two families meet in the morning at the Parc de la Tête d’Or, in front of the old lime tree. Nobody refused.

There were almost thirty of them in front of the tree that morning. Romanians, Spaniards, French people, and Mr Fournier, the gardener, who had put on a tie for the occasion. On the bark of the lime tree you could still see the two letters carved in 1962: “H ♥ H”. Doña Carmen asked Lucia what those letters meant. Lucia told her the story in a few sentences. Doña Carmen crossed herself.

Odile went up to the tree and put her hand on the bark. Then she whistled the waltz, softly, as every morning for a year. Rose-Hélène, in Julien’s arms, took Henri’s harmonica out of her pocket and blew the first three notes. And, to everyone’s surprise, don Manuel opened his guitar case.

He had never heard the waltz. He listened to it once, all the way through, whistled by Odile. Then he played it. Not exactly as Henri had written it: with Spanish chords, a slightly warmer rhythm, notes that sounded like an Andalusian sun. But it was definitely Henri’s waltz. Odile listened with her eyes closed. “Henri would have loved it,” she murmured. “He always wanted to go to Spain.”

While don Manuel played, the grandmother and doña Carmen took each other’s hand, without even realising it. Elena was already crying, though the wedding hadn’t even begun. Dan took his speech out of his pocket and read it again, for the twentieth time, moving his lips. Mr Fournier, for his part, was looking at the branches of the lime tree, where the first May leaves had just appeared.

Before leaving, Mr Fournier took Julien aside. He announced, with a gardener’s quiet pride, that the twelve little lime trees grown from Henri and Hélène’s tree had all survived the winter. They were now almost a metre tall. They would be ready to plant in the autumn, in ten cities, if the ministry wished. Julien wrote the date in his notebook, next to Sami’s drawing.

In the evening, when everyone had gone home, Ioana asked Radu to walk with her to the bench at Fourvière, the one at the care home, where Hélène had spent so many afternoons. It was mild. Below them the city was lighting up, light after light. They sat side by side, brother and sister, as when they were children on the balcony in Iași.

Ioana took out of her bag a yellowed envelope, tied with a small piece of blue ribbon. On the envelope, in shaky handwriting, was written: “For Radu, on his wedding day. To be opened the day before.” Radu looked at it without understanding. “Hélène gave it to me in April last year,” Ioana explained. “She made me promise to keep it. She was sure you would marry Lucia. She said she had known it from the first day.”

Radu opened the envelope with trembling hands. Inside was a single sheet, written in blue pen, in large careful letters. He read it aloud, slowly, because his sister had the right to hear it: “My dear Radu. Tomorrow you are going to say yes. Say it loudly, so that everyone hears it. I was never able to say it. So say it a little for me too.”

“Don’t try to be perfect. Henri wasn’t perfect, and I loved him all my life. Just be present. Listen to her when she talks, even when she talks too much. And when you quarrel, which will happen, remember that a waltz is danced by two, and that the one who steps back allows the other to move forward. With all my tenderness. Hélène.”

Radu folded the sheet and put it back in the envelope. He said nothing for a long time. Below, on the Saône, a riverboat went by, lit up, with music. Ioana rested her head on the shoulder of her little brother, who wasn’t so little any more. “You know what?” he said at last. “Tomorrow I’m going to say it so loudly that she’ll hear it, up there.”

On the eve of the wedding, Radu receives three messages about the same thing, in three different registers. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.

The first message is from Chloé, his former fellow intern: “Hi, groom-to-be! You ready? Tomorrow we’re gonna party till the end of the night. Can’t wait. And don’t worry, I won’t scoff all the cake. Hugs!”

The second is from Nathalie Fabre, his boss: “Good evening Radu, I wanted to let you know that the whole office will be there tomorrow. We are very happy for you and Lucia. Enjoy this beautiful day. See you tomorrow. Nathalie.”

The third comes from the mayor’s office: “Sir, we have the honour of confirming that your marriage ceremony will be held tomorrow, Saturday 4 May, at three p.m. precisely. You are kindly requested to present yourself a quarter of an hour in advance, bearing an identity document.”

Radu smiled as he read the three messages. They said almost the same thing: “We’ll be there tomorrow.” But each said it in its own way. Chloé talked like a friend, Nathalie like a boss who liked him, and the town hall like… a town hall.

He replied to all three. To Chloé he wrote: “Totally ready! See you tomorrow!” To Nathalie: “Thank you very much, Nathalie, see you tomorrow.” And to the town hall he wrote three very polite lines, checking twice that he hadn’t left out a single “ne”.

Then he got a fourth message, from his grandmother, in Romanian, without punctuation: “ai mâncat” (have you eaten). For that one he didn’t need any register. He simply replied: “Da, bunico.” (Yes, Grandma.) And he went to eat a sarma.
À quelle heure Radu doit-il se présenter à la mairie ?
